Chapter 32

Companions, presence, the join page and settings

The member list with roles and “here now”; the owner’s invite link and two moderation buttons; presence chips fed by the live query; the join page as one query and one form; and the settings page — an owner-only page, a form that reads its props once, single-flight refresh, and a delete that asks first.

By the end of this chapter

Finish the trip’s social surface: everything a person can do to another person on the trip, and the page an owner uses to change the trip itself.

The last tab and the two pages around it. Nothing here introduces a new library; it is the remote functions from chapter 20 with faces, and the interesting parts are the choices about which write is a form and which is a command.

Making an invite is a command because the result exists to be copied — a link, on screen, with a button that writes it to the clipboard. Leaving is a form, because it is a page with a button and should work with JavaScript off. here is a set derived from the presence list, so the chip beside a companion who has the trip open appears and disappears with the stream. That chip is the only one in the sea colour — presence is live, and the sea already means live — while the role beside it is a fact, so a quiet chip. After a copy the button shows a check for 1.6 seconds and the toast says “Copied”; the toast is a live region already, so the button carries none of its own, which used to make a screen reader say it twice.

Presence is an overlapping stack of initials, one circle per other person, with the stop under their pointer in the tooltip, fed entirely by view.presence — which the server refreshes from its thirty-second time-to-live. Four faces, then a “+N”: a crowd is a number, not a row of circles — and the people behind it are still in the list, in a visually hidden “and 2 more: Ana and Cal” built with Intl.ListFormat, because a list named “here now” has to contain everybody who is. The name beside each circle shows from 48em and is visually hidden below it, so a screen reader and the end-to-end test still find it. The initials are computed from the name; there are no avatars in this app, and a coloured circle with two letters is what a person recognises across a table. Nobody arrives with a bounce: a chip appearing is information, and a chip bouncing is a slot machine.

The join page

One query says whether the link still works; one remote form accepts it. The page is under (app), so a stranger is sent to sign in and brought back here afterwards — the invite test in chapter 43 follows exactly that path with a brand-new account. Every state the invite can be in has a sentence: already a member, used, expired, or a button.

Settings: owner only

The remote function already refuses to *change* anything for anybody but the owner. This page refuses to *show* itself, with a 403 rather than a 404, because a member who is not the owner already knows the trip exists — error() in markup, which SvelteKit turns into the right status on the server and the error page in the browser, where +error.svelte prints the sentence from page.error.message. That sentence is m.error_owner_only(), a Paraglide message: the error page prints it word for word, so a literal would have put an English sentence under a German heading. The slug is params.slug from PageProps, as on the trip page. Both declarations are $derived, so they follow the query: when the form below saves, the server refreshes tripBySlug in the same response, and trip — and everything drawn from it, the form’s heading and the embed section that only offers its code for a trip visible by link — is the saved trip. The first version read the query two ways, a template await for the first render and query.current for the embed section, and the comment that justified it outlived the code it described; one reactive read, declared once, is the version with nothing to keep in step.

The fields start from the trip and belong to the form from then on: untrack reads the prop once, on purpose, and the page keys the form on the slug so a different trip is a different form. This is the *other* answer to the stop dialog’s question — assignable deriveds reset on a prop change; untrack says the prop never changes — and each is right where it is used. The save is a command with .updates(tripBySlug(trip.slug)): single-flight from the client’s side, naming the query this page is holding so the server refreshes it in the same response and the embed section below sees the new visibility before the toast appears.

Delete is a remote form whose question is asked inside enhance, the remote form’s own hook. With JavaScript off the form posts and the trip is gone; with it on, enhance is handed the form and submits it only if confirm() says yes. The first version put the confirm() in an onsubmit and called preventDefault() on a no — the way you would cancel a plain form — and “Cancel” deleted the trip anyway: the remote form’s attachment has a submit listener of its own, and it does not look at defaultPrevented. The end-to-end suite now dismisses the dialog first and checks the trip is still listed, then accepts it and checks it is gone (chapter 43). This is the one destructive *form* in the app; the smaller removals — a stop, an expense, a companion — are commands behind a button, with the person looking at the thing they remove, and ask nothing. It is a component of its own so the page can put it last, under the embed section: the one thing on the page that cannot be undone comes after everything that can, where nobody reaches it on the way to something else. Its heading is an h2 at an h3’s size, so heading navigation files the danger zone as a section of its own and not as a part of the embed section above it.

Checkpoint

  • You can say why the invite is a command and leaving is a form.
  • You can explain the settings page’s 403 and where error() in markup is handled.
  • You can compare untrack in the settings form with assignable deriveds in the stop dialog and say when each is right.
  • You can say why a confirm() belongs in a remote form’s enhance and not in an onsubmit with preventDefault().
